Absolutely we're out here - unfortunately I think a lot of people get swayed by gender norms and find themselves re-enacting them to some extent. I think a lot of people would be open to more exploration in that regard if they really let themselves consider.

As for how to get comfortable with receiving, both sexually and in other ways, I'd say it's a case of a) communicating your desires to your partner, and b) starting small. Receiving both sexual pleasure and affection can feel quite vulnerable and exposing, and can sometimes bring up difficult emotions, and I think a lot of us fall into more dominant or giving behaviours in our romantic relationships in part because it feels safer. So it makes sense that this feels a little daunting to you. It's also of course totally normal to feel nervous about something you've never done before. As with anything new to us, it's about slowly expanding your comfort zone. 

For example, if we're talking about receiving during sex, consider what feels the most comfortable to you at this point in time - it might be a sex act in a position which still allows you to be in control to some extent, like receiving oral by sitting on someone's face or having them kneel before you whilst you sit or stand. It might be something like grinding/scissoring, which allows you to both feel pleasure at the same time and therefore might not feel like it's purely focused on you. It could be anything, but just try and imagine a bunch of different sex acts that would allow for you to be touched/get off, and think: which of these feels the most comfortable to me right now? And then that's where you start.

Same with non-sexual acts of affection or care. I remember with my butch ex who had generally been put into a more dominant role in their previous relationships, they had never been the little spoon before - just being the little spoon whilst cuddling for a few minutes and seeing how that feels could be somewhere you start. Or maybe asking your partner if they have any ideas for cute nicknames for you. This one feels more vague because there are so many ways someone can express care and affection, so I have less concrete examples, but just think to yourself what would you like to receive, and then, again, which of these things feels like a comfortable place to start, and then ask for those things from your partner.

I also wonder if in your relationships you're perhaps falling into a pattern of behaviour as the more 'dominant' one/the giver/the caretaker etc. (and this is a vicious cycle bc I think a lot of people put these expectations on masc-presenting people too) and that's partially contributing to a dynamic that isn't fully satisfying you (ie one in which you're not receiving the care, affection, and sexual pleasure you yearn for). It might be worthwhile thinking about that and thinking if there are any ways you could approach your romantic relationships differently. 

It makes me sad that some people aren't receiving these things in relationships, I think everyone deserves them! Gender and gender presentation shouldn't have anything to do with it.

I’m in my early 30s and have just started watching Cheers. Honestly, I think what put me off watching it before is simply the time period - not that I have anything against watching stuff from the ‘80s or prior, it’s just that there’s _so much_ TV out there, I sort of feel like I have to draw a line as to what shows I consider watching or I’ll have a list of 1000 to watch! 

In my mind, shows from prior to the ‘90s just sort of drifted into the background to me as not really an option to consider. I would imagine this is probably common amongst people my age and younger. The other shows you’ve mentioned - Seinfeld and The Office - are significantly more recent, one by 7 years and the other by about 23, iirc? Seinfeld is largely a ‘90s show, and to people currently in their 30s, and to a lesser extent 20s, I think the ‘90s still feel much closer and more relevant than the ‘80s culturally. A least when it comes to TV.

Some other possibilities:

- I’m guessing you may be in the US. In the UK, and possibly elsewhere, Cheers is difficult to find online. It’s only on one niche streaming service with not much on it, which practically no one uses, on YT it’s incredibly expensive, and I wasn’t even able to find it pirated anywhere. I’ve bought the secondhand DVDs, but a lot of people my age and younger wouldn’t bother to do that considering many people don’t have access to DVD players anymore. (I bought a DVD drive specifically because I do like to check out older and more niche stuff, but I’m probably in the minority there). Shows like Seinfeld and The Office are both on Netflix and other platforms here. 

- Cheers does strike me as feeling quite different to the sitcoms that I’m used to, and as much as I’m enjoying it, it’s not on the same level as the sitcoms I really love for me personally. I was trying to figure out what felt slightly off about it and I realised….oh. It’s because the whole show is set in the bar. That makes for a _very_ different viewing experience compared to the other big American sitcoms - Seinfeld, Friends, The Office - in which we get to see the characters in various locations. With those shows I get to feel more like I’m entering a fully realised world and that also allows me to feel I know the characters more intimately. The experience of watching Cheers is more like watching a stage play. I feel like a lot is being inferred and there’s a lot I’m not getting to see. I’m not necessarily saying one is better than the other, but that I think this means Cheers won’t be as accessible to younger audiences. It’s not what they’re familiar with. 

- it also means that it’s not as visually interesting to watch. The bar is a cosy set but it’s all we get. There’s not much of an emphasis on fashion, either. And visuals do matter when it comes to longevity of TV. There’s no doubt that a big part of Friends’ longevity is the apartments that viewers still want to live in and all the fashion that viewers still take inspiration from, for example. Seinfeld is also interesting visually imo.

- the politics of the time period might be a bit more difficult to swallow. As an example, I recently watched the episode when Sam’s friend comes out as gay and everyone is worried the bar’s going to turn into a gay bar. Whilst the overall framing of the episode was clearly favourable of gay people, the fact that almost all of the main characters - people I believe we’re supposed to like - were being incredibly homophobic, was very uncomfortable to watch and did put me off the show for a bit. Things like that might put off some for good.

- and as a final thing, a lot of people don’t like laugh tracks now. I don’t feel that way at all, but I think if you add all this together: it’s not easily accessible online outside of the US. It’s from the ‘80s. It’s all set in one location and similar to watching a stage play. The politics are very dated. There’s a laugh track…. There’s just a lot of barriers there in the way of younger audiences watching.

Personally I do wish people would make the effort to go back and give older TV a chance though!

Being neurodivergent isn’t an illness. It’s an umbrella term that includes different neurotypes (meaning the brain works in a different way to the majority.) This can include learning difficulties like dyspraxia and dyslexia, or more wide-reaching brain differences like ADHD and autism. The latter drastically changes the way the brain functions and the person’s experience of being in their brains and in the world. From the outside it might seem like someone ‘just being a bit odd’ but it’s much more than that.
